You've been saying dhuwala since Lesson 2. Time to meet its whole family, because pointing, in Gupapuyŋu, is a full grammatical system.

Three distances, not two. English has this/that. Gupapuyŋu has:
dhuwala → this (right here, near me)
dhuwali → that (near you)
ŋunha → that yonder (away from us both)

Three zones: mine, yours, beyond. The space between speakers is mapped before anything is even said about it. (Japanese speakers, hello again: これ/それ/あれ, kore/sore/are, the exact same three-way split.)

And the places to match:
dhiyala → here
dhiyali → there (by you)
ŋunhili → there yonder

Barpuru ŋayi ga nhina dhiyala bala'ŋura → Yesterday he was here in this hut
Yolŋu ŋunha rirrikthun ga wäŋiya → There's a person sick over there in the camp

And movement toward: dhipala → onto this / to here:
Rulwaŋdhurru dhipala tablelili → Put it on this table

Now the part that makes this a system and not a word list: demonstratives take case, just like nouns. When this-one does something, wants something, or owns the action, the pointer itself inflects:

dhiyaŋu → this one (as doer, ergative)
dhiyaki → for this one (dative)
ŋuriŋi → that one (as doer)

Dhiyaŋi miyalkthu nhanŋu ŋatha gäŋala nhanukuŋu → THAT woman took his food from him (the demonstrative AND the noun both carry the doer-marking)
Dhiyaki ŋarra djälnydja → It's THIS one I want

Same logic you learned in Lesson 11, applied to the pointing words. Nothing new to memorise, just the suffix system reaching one more word class.

One more secret: Gupapuyŋu has no word for the. And it doesn't need one, because dhuwala / dhuwali / ŋunhi do that work. When a story keeps referring back to someone already mentioned, ŋunhi steps in: that (aforementioned) one. English the is just a demonstrative that went pale with overuse; here the pointing stays vivid.

Think about why a land-based oral culture would grow THREE distances and case-marked pointers. Because where something sits, relative to me, to you, to the country, is never incidental information. It's the first fact. The grammar points before it describes.
